paras: The threatened lynching of Robert Smith occurred in Talbot County, Maryland, in late August 1915, when residents around Royal Oak uttered threats against Smith, a Black youth jailed at Easton on a charge of assaulting a young white girl. Talk of lynching subsided after State's Attorney Charles J. Butler had a special grand jury called, and Smith was indicted, granted a change of venue, and tried at Elkton in September. Papers in four states and Alexandria carried the case, several pairing it with the hanging of "Wish" Sheppard at Denton that week.

Smith, described as "colored" and 16 or 17, had worked for the Denny family since he was a small child. The girl, Annabel Denny, was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Elbert L. Denny of near Royal Oak, a family the Richmond Virginian called one of the oldest and most prominent in Talbot County. The charge came as Aloysius "Wish" Sheppard, convicted of assaulting a farmer's daughter near Federalsburg, was hanged at Denton.

According to the girl's account, she was reading in her father's ground-floor bedroom one night when Smith entered, threw her on the bed and stifled her screams. Her father, who had been away, was reported ready to shoot Smith, but kept the matter quiet until her mother preferred the charge at Easton on Thursday night. Early on August 27, Sheriff Sewell and Deputy Sheriff Stevens arrested Smith in bed at his home, and after a hearing before Police Justice Tharp he was locked up at Easton "for safe-keeping."

A Baltimore dispatch reported that "mob violence is feared," and the Alexandria Gazette described the Royal Oak neighborhood as aroused, with threats uttered against the accused. Butler went to Centreville to ask Judge Hopper to recall the grand jury, and a wire dispatch credited the step with averting the danger that a mob would seize and lynch Smith. By August 30 a Wilmington paper reported that the assurance had stopped "all incipient talk of lynching," though Sheriff Sewell kept watch so that no crowds would loiter around the jail.

Judge Hopper had the grand jury convened in special session, and early in September it indicted Smith, named as "James R. Smith," for criminal assault, a charge that carried the death penalty. The attendance at court was very large, but the Evening Journal saw no disorder.

At a special court session at Easton on September 10, Smith's counsel, George H. Pendleton, a Black lawyer from Baltimore, filed Smith's affidavit that he could not get a fair and impartial trial in Talbot County. The court removed the case to Cecil County, where Smith was tried at Elkton on September 24 under the statute on carnal knowledge of a girl under 14. The judges reserved their verdict until Monday; the Evening Journal expected his youth to spare him the death penalty, and no report of the verdict was found.

All coverage came from white newspapers, and several headlines treated the accusation as established: "LITTLE GIRL IS VICTIM OF FIEND" (Richmond Virginian), "OUTRAGEOUS CRIME" (Middletown Transcript), "BY COLORED BOY" (Evening Journal). The Philadelphia Evening Public Ledger instead put the threat at the center with "Quells Mob's Fury to Lynch," while the Evening Journal and the Middletown Transcript quoted Butler that he anticipated "nothing like mob violence." Under the headline "Met With Swift Justice," the Newark Post set the case beside Sheppard's hanging, observing that despite that punishment public feeling was "wrought up."

Later reports, carried mainly by the Evening Journal and Delaware and Maryland weeklies, followed the court proceedings. The Evening Journal's last report, "HIS YOUTH MAY SAVE HIM FROM GALLOWS," stressed Smith's age and his long service with the Dennys.

Reports differed on the girl's age, with early accounts giving 15 and the indictment and court reports giving 13, or "under 14" in the Cecil Whig's description of the charge. The first Easton report placed the alleged assault on the Tuesday night before August 28, whereas the indictment gave August 22. The accused also appears as Robert Smith, James R. Smith, Robert J. Smith and James Robert Smith. Butler himself was reported to doubt from the evidence whether the assault had been "entirely complete."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Smith
bases: Residents near Royal Oak threatened a Black youth held in the Easton jail and a dispatch spoke of danger that a mob would seize and lynch him, but no attack on the jail was reported (A2, A3, A6).

Smith was not killed; the coverage reports threats and talk of lynching driven by the assault charge, which ended once a special grand jury was promised, and he was indicted and tried in court (A3, A6, A9, A14).

Separate reports from Easton and Baltimore agree on the charge, the arrest and the fear of mob violence (A2, A3, A5, A6), though the State's Attorney was quoted as expecting no mob violence (A4, A11).

accounts.label: Easton and wire reports
accounts.gist: Feeling around Royal Oak ran so high, with threats uttered, that a mob might seize and lynch Smith; the promise of a special grand jury quieted it.

accounts.label: State's Attorney Butler
accounts.gist: Butler said he anticipated nothing like mob violence because the people of the county would let the law take its course, but still pressed for a speedy trial.

accounts.label: The girl's account
accounts.gist: She said Smith entered her father's ground-floor bedroom while she was reading, threw her on the bed and stifled her screams.

accounts.label: Defense affidavit
accounts.gist: Smith swore he did not believe he could get a fair and impartial trial in Talbot County.

framing.detail: The Richmond Virginian's 'LITTLE GIRL IS VICTIM OF FIEND' and the Middletown Transcript's 'OUTRAGEOUS CRIME' treated the charge as proven.
The Public Ledger's 'Quells Mob's Fury to Lynch' credited the prosecutor's speed with averting a lynching.
The Wilmington Evening Journal headlined 'BY COLORED BOY' and called the case a crime like Sheppard's, then followed the court case to 'HIS YOUTH MAY SAVE HIM FROM GALLOWS'.
The Newark Post's 'Met With Swift Justice' set the case beside Sheppard's hanging and reported public feeling 'wrought up'.

conflicts.note: The indictment and court reports (13, under 14) are the better evidence on the charge.
Aug. 22, 1915, was a Sunday; the indictment date comes from the court record.
Probably one man; court reports use James R. / James Robert.
